1. ARIMA vs. ETS

library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
# A tibble: 1 × 1
  .gaps
  <lgl>
1 FALSE
liquor |> 
  autoplot(sales) +
  labs(x = "Month", 
       y = "Liquor Sales (Millions of Dollars)", 
       title = "US Retail Liquor Sales by Month (1992-2019)")
gg_season(liquor, y = log(sales)) +
  labs(x = "Month", 
       y = "Log Sales", 
       title = "Logged US Retail Liquor Store Sales by Month (1992-2019)")

There is a clear upward sloping trend and seasonal pattern, with sales increasing more or less linearly over time, and a big spike every year in December. Sales are typically lowest in Jan/Feb and highest in December, and the size of the seasonal swings grows with the level, so this series is a good candidate for a log transformation.

liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

An ARIMA(1, 0, 2)(2, 1, 1)[12] model was chosen, meaning that there is one seasonal difference applied to the series. An ETS(A, A, A), an additive Holt-Winters model was chosen. The 3 A’s mean that the model uses additive errors, trends, and seasonal components.

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()
liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
# A tibble: 1 × 3

1 arima     120.         0

Yes, the residuals look vaguely like white noise, but the L-B test rejects the null with a p-value of essentially 0, meaning that we reject the assumption of white noise. There is still leftover structure in the residuals.

liquor_cv <- liquor |>
  stretch_tsibble(.init = 120, .step = 1) |>
  filter(.id < max(.id))

liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

saveRDS(liquor_cv_fit, "results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

There will be 216 different forecast origins considered. We have 28 years of monthly data, and 10 of those years make the first training sample and the first forecast origin. We then have 18 years of monthly data -> 18x12 = 216 origins, plus the first forecast origin minus the dropped December 2019 origin.

liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

January 2002 is the first forecast and December 2019 is the last. The ARIMA model forecast the most accurately, having both the lowest MAE and RMSE.

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$ets
DM = -2.9062, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value =
0.004042
alternative hypothesis: two.sided
forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive, h = 1, power = 2)

    Diebold-Mariano Test

data:  liquor_errs$arimaliquor_errs$snaive
DM = -10.755, Forecast horizon = 1, Loss function power = 2, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

ARIMA vs. ETS: DM of -2.9062, p-value of 0.004042
ARIMA vs. SRW: DM of -10.755, p-value of 2.2e-16

The Diebold-Mariano tests confirm that the differences in forecast errors were significant. ARIMA is better than both at the 1% significance level. If I were the liquor store, I would want to use the ARIMA model.

2. Forecast Combination

liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
.model .type RMSE MAE
arima Test 81.43 65.65
combo Test 85.19 66.77
ets Test 94.35 72.31
snaive Test 161.26 136.63

Combo does better than the SRW and ETS models, but worse than the ARIMA model.

cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
[1] 0.8782931

The combination does not beat the ARIMA model because the ARIMA and ETS errors are highly correlated, and because the ETS is statistically significantly less accurate than the ARIMA. The correlation coefficient of 0.878 is quite high, meaning that the models missed many of the same forecasts, and the combined models errors are basically an average of the ARIMA’s errors + the errors of the less accurate ETS.

3. VAR vs. BVAR

qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))

growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

We will produce 120 forecasts for each variable (4 Quarterly forecasts for each of the 30 years from 1990 to 2019). The first forecast will be for Q1 of 1990, and the last will be for Q4 of 2019.

var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)            # columns: y_t, then its lags 1 to p
  M <- ncol(z)                    # number of variables
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))   # constant, latest p lags
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL
for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

rmse_by_var(fc_var1)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5130384 0.4598547 2.4927057 0.1956584 0.2084055 0.1988068 0.3902989 0.3610310 
rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
      gdp      cons       inv       emp      infl    unrate       ffr      gs10 
0.5693241 0.5268484 2.5212629 0.2277561 0.2069608 0.2153966 0.4973504 0.3789663

The VAR(1) forecasts more accurately for 7/8 of the variables. Since VAR(1) is the special case of VAR(4) where the coeffficients on lags 2, 3, and 4 are equal to 0, it will fit as least as good as the VAR(1) in sample, and this might mean that the VAR(4) is overfitting the training data. The increased estimation error created by estimating 4 lags outweighs any benefits of potentially decreased approximation error.

bvar_cv <- function(lambda) {
  pr <- bv_priors(hyper = "lambda",
                  mn = bv_mn(lambda = bv_lambda(mode = lambda, sd = 0.4,
                                                min = 0.999 * lambda,
                                                max = 1.001 * lambda),
                             b = 0))
  fc <- NULL
  for (T in origins) {
    fit_T <- bvar(y[1:T, ], lags = 4, priors = pr,
                  n_draw = 2000, n_burn = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
    x <- c(1, t(y[T:(T - 3), ]))         # constant and 4 lags of each variable
    fc <- rbind(fc, x %*% coef(fit_T))   # forecast of y_{T+1}
  }
  fc
}

set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_03 <- bvar_cv(0.3)
saveRDS(fc_bvar_03, "results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

set.seed(422)
fc_bvar_005 <- bvar_cv(0.05)

var_results <- tibble(
  Variable = colnames(y),
  `VAR(1)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var1),
  `VAR(4)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var4),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_03),
  `BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05` = rmse_by_var(fc_bvar_005)
)

saveRDS(var_results, "results/var_results.rds")
readRDS("results/var_results.rds") |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
Variable VAR(1) VAR(4) BVAR(4), lambda = 0.3 BVAR(4), lambda = 0.05
gdp 0.513 0.569 0.539 0.567
cons 0.460 0.527 0.486 0.495
inv 2.493 2.521 2.385 2.698
emp 0.196 0.228 0.211 0.315
infl 0.208 0.207 0.197 0.330
unrate 0.199 0.215 0.203 0.216
ffr 0.390 0.497 0.414 0.358
gs10 0.361 0.379 0.359 0.362

The BVAR(4) with lambda = 0.3 does better than the VAR(4) for all of the variables. The difference is explained by the shrinkage performed in the BVAR, which is reducing our estimation error.

It does worse than the VAR(1) for 5/8 of the variables, which could be an indicator that the additional lags are introducing more estimation error than useful information.

When lamba = 0.05, it performs worse for everything except the ffr variable, which tells us that we should not be shrinnking this aggressively. I think that saying that the winners RMSE is a fair estimate of future forecast accuracy is too optimistic, because it could have just gotten lucky in this training sample. We tested four different models across 8 variables, so there is a good chance some of the low RMSE’s are just due to chance.

e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

v2e_var4 <- actual[, "inv"] - fc_var4[, 3]
v2e_bvar <- actual[, "inv"] - fc_bvar_03[, 3]

Based on the DM tests, we reject the null for GDP, and fail to reject the null for the INV variable. This means that the accuracy gap is real for GDP, but we cannot distinguish between the two models for INV. This reinforces how I felt about the results for 4.3b, as it shows how one of the cases where it appeared the VAR(1) was more accurate did not hold up through the DM test.

4. Factor Model

md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])
md <- md_raw[-1, ] |> mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,                      # level
         "2" = d(x),                   # first difference
         "3" = d(d(x)),                # second difference
         "4" = log(x),                 # log
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),        # growth rate
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),     # change in the growth rate
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
[1] 718 122
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
  INDPRO   PAYEMS CPIAUCSL FEDFUNDS 
       5        5        6        2

INDPRO and PAYEMS are transformed into their growth rates, CPIAUCSL is transformed into the change in the growth rate, and FEDFUNDS is transformed with a first difference. The Federal Funds rate is transformed differently because it is a rate that sits around a consistent range, and it is more useful to look at the change in that rate rather than the growth rate of that rate. The Industrial Production Index is transformed using the growth rate because it is easier to interpret the growth rate of industrial production, rather than the difference in the index, which is hard to contextualize because of the units.

The first factor captures the production side of the economy. It is highly correlated with multiple series tracking employment and industrial production.

The second factor captures price indexes/inflation. It is highly correlated with multiple series tracking consumption via the CPI.

ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
  RMSE_AR   RMSE_FA 
0.6168431 0.5887272

Numbers are the same as we got in class. If we first estimated the factors using the whole sample and then used them in the horse race, this would be cheating because we are using data that we would not have actually known at the time, aka creating data leakage.

direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
# A tibble: 1 × 7
  series   forecasts RMSE_AR RMSE_FA MAE_AR MAE_FA DM_pvalue
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>   <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>     <dbl>
1 CPIAUCSL       349    2.11    1.89   1.58   1.35  0.000443

Yes, the factors improve the forecast, reducing RMSE by ~10.3%. This difference is statistically significant at any realistic significance level, with a p-value of 0.0004, meaning that we can reject the null of equal accuracy.

5. Reflection

One trend that I noticed throughout was that you have to be very intentional when making your forecasting model more complex. For example, in the combinations section we saw that you can’t take two forecasts you created and blindly combine them, because you may create worse forecasts even though your model looks more sophisticated. We also saw this when comparing the VAR(1), VAR(4), and the two BVAR models: the introduction of extra lags hurts with the VAR(4), and a bad lambda value hurts as well, both need to be picked intentionally. It seems like simple models are hard to beat when your data has a relatively stable trend, as the simple models pick this up well without introducing the added noise of extra lags, variables, etc. Shrinkage, equal weights, and factors are all methods that try to turn complicated models back into simple models, keeping the benefits of the simplicity while picking up additional benefit that the extra data adds.
